A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ML-Agent and retain identifiable methods, experiments and case studies. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: v1 reports original ML-Agent benchmark results, training and reward ablations, scaling analyses and execution case studies in Section 5 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark comparisons and ablations, including five additional held-out tasks and cost analyses in Appendix C.

M1.justification: Equation 6 replaces rewards of 0 for errors, 0.5 for neutral outcomes and sigmoid-scaled improvements with -1, 0 and linear normalized improvements. Section 4.1 and Algorithm 1 also describe category-specific action pools selected through farthest-point sampling, replacing the earlier flat top-ten diversity selection, although Appendix B.3 retains the older description. These are substantive reported procedure revisions; the PDFs do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: The original training and evaluation tasks remain. Appendix C.3/Table 12 adds APTOS blindness detection, H&M recommendations, Optiver trading regression, Right Whale Redux audio classification and English text normalization. These introduce medical imagery, multimodal recommendations, time series, audio and normalization tasks beyond the original coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands from MLAB and AIDE to include ML-Master, with new Qwen3-235B, GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro comparisons. AIDE also gains a Qwen2.5-7B control. The corresponding main comparison drops MLAB's Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o entries and AIDE's GPT-4o/o1-preview entries, although some older models remain in other plots.

E3.justification: Primary result tables switch from raw average/best scores to percentage gain over initial scripts, a metric already used elsewhere in v1. v2 adds per-trajectory dollar cost and estimated amortization metrics. The reported training budgets and 15-step/30-minute trajectory limits remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Table 2 newly reports removing the entire reward module alongside summaries of existing fine-tuning and step-wise RL comparisons. The reward-component ablation expands from five to eight retained tasks. Figure 2 and Appendix C.4 add performance-cost and amortization analyses. Earlier diversity, scaling, thought and case-study analyses are substantially retained.

E5.justification: v1's main table reports averages and best scores without uncertainty estimates; v2 Table 1 adds ± terms throughout the per-task comparisons. Both report eight evaluation trajectories, so additional runs are not established. v2 does not identify whether the ± terms represent standard deviations, standard errors or confidence intervals.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive baseline, additional-task, ablation and cost results. Table 1 reports overall average gains of 16.40% for ML-Agent and 20.95% for AIDE–GPT-5. Tables 13–14 estimate $322.81 in pre-inference costs and 1,518–4,262 trajectories to amortize them. Many retained scores are converted to relative gains; those conversions do not establish improved same-setting performance.

T1.justification: Section 3 revises the formal state from feedback-only history to the initial task specification plus action-feedback history. Appendix A changes finite-horizon product and summation bounds and removes an outer time sum in Equation 10. These are localized formal revisions within the retained MDP derivation, without a new theorem or guarantee.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes outperforming DeepSeek-R1 and achieving state-of-the-art performance across 13 tasks. v2's abstract and conclusion emphasize competitiveness with GPT-5 at much lower computational cost, positioning a trained small model as an alternative to proprietary agents. The learning-based paradigm and three-component framework remain core contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds an economic interpretation of the results, including the deployment volume needed to offset training costs in Appendix C.4. Section 5.1 explicitly justifies non-exhaustive benchmark evaluation and asserts scalability with additional compute. Conversely, v1's explicit warning that generalization to entirely new ML frameworks or architectures remains unresolved is removed.

D1.justification: v2 adds trajectory-generation pseudocode, sentence-transformer/FPS implementation information, the GPT-5 version identifier and cost-accounting details. Hardware, learning rates, batch sizes and detailed case-study code remain substantially unchanged. The project repository link provided on v1's first page is omitted in v2.

R1.justification: Related work adds ML-Master, AutoML-Agent, small-model and agentic-RL surveys, and references for newer evaluated backbones, while removing SELA and several older citations. Cost and accessibility receive more emphasis, but the established AutoML/ML-agent/RL organization and learning-versus-prompting novelty position remain.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations, experimental narrative and conclusion undergo substantial rewriting or condensation. Section 5.3 is reorganized, Appendices B and C gain subsections, and case studies move from C.3 to C.5. The separate limitations and broader-impact discussions disappear, with a generic Impact Statement added.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from one-column to two-column layout. The interaction overview and AIDE radar chart are removed; the training diagram is retained and renumbered. A performance-cost scatterplot, algorithm display and new tables are added. Main comparison and ablation tables are extensively restructured, and appendix prompt boxes are restyled.

improvement.justification: The broader comparisons reveal competitive limitations, five additional tasks test previously uncovered generalization settings, and cost amortization makes the efficiency claim more assessable. These improve the empirical assessment and qualify earlier superiority claims. However, conflicting action-pool descriptions, undefined uncertainty terms, and removal of the repository link and explicit cross-environment limitation weaken clarity and reproducibility, limiting the overall gain.
